# METHODOLOGY

This chapter explains how the study answers its research questions. It describes how the posts are collected and annotated, how the models are trained and compared, and how the benchmarking system and the prototype web application are built and tested.

## Research Methodology

This study follows the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) of Peffers et al. [-@peffers2007design]. DSRM is a methodology for design science research, which creates and evaluates artifacts intended to solve identified problems [@peffers2007design]. The study uses DSRM because its main contribution is an artifact, a multi-task model that performs humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts. It also contributes a second artifact, a Taglish typhoon dataset annotated for both tasks, on which the model is trained.

The study carries out the six activities of DSRM in order [@peffers2007design]. The first two activities, identifying the problem and defining the objectives of a solution, take place in Chapter 1. During design and development, the study builds the dataset and designs the multi-task model. It then uses the validation set to select one of 13 multi-task optimizers, and the model trained with this optimizer becomes the final model. During demonstration, the study uses the final model in a prototype web application that performs humanitarian classification and NER on posts. During evaluation, the study compares the final model with two single-task models, one for each task, on the test set. It also measures the agreement between the annotators to evaluate the dataset. During communication, the study reports its results in this thesis and releases the final model, the code, and the post IDs of the dataset.

## Subjects of the Study

The subjects of this study are the dataset it builds and the models it trains. The dataset consists of approximately 2,500 Taglish posts on X about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. The posts come from one day before to three days after the period each tropical cyclone spent within the Philippine Area of Responsibility, based on the dates in the tropical cyclone preliminary reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. Each post is annotated for both tasks, with one of the ten humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid] for humanitarian classification and with the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner] for NER.

The study trains 15 models on the dataset, two single-task models and 13 multi-task models. All of them start from the same pretrained transformer encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M [@aisingapore2026sealion]. One single-task model performs humanitarian classification, and one performs NER. The 13 multi-task models share the same architecture and differ only in the multi-task optimizer used to train them. Each multi-task model is compared with the single-task models to measure its negative transfer. After training, one multi-task model is selected as the final model based on its negative transfer on the validation set (Section 3.6). The final model is then compared with the single-task models on the test set, on F1-scores and computational cost.

The 13 multi-task optimizers are chosen by two criteria. First, each optimizer was evaluated in at least two of the empirical studies of multi-task optimizers reviewed in Chapter 2, following Kurin et al. [-@kurin2022unitary], who compared well-established optimizers. Second, each optimizer can be trained with the same model and training setup as the others, so that only the optimizer differs. The 13 optimizers in @tbl-complexity are all those that meet both criteria.

## Sampling Technique

The sampling frame consists of the posts on X that match the keywords (Section 3.5) and fall within the collection window of each tropical cyclone (Section 3.2). Where the windows of two tropical cyclones overlap, they are merged so that no post is collected twice.

The language of each word in a post is identified as English, Tagalog, or other with the dictionary-based method of Herrera et al. [-@herrera2022tweettaglish], and a post is included when it has at least one English word and one Tagalog word. Reposts, quotes, and exact and near-duplicate posts are excluded.

About 2,500 posts are sampled for annotation by stratified sampling, with each day of the collection windows contributing posts in proportion to the number of posts on it that match the keywords. The sample size is based on resource constraints [@lakens2022sample], because about 2,500 posts is the most that two annotators can label in 2 to 3 hours a day over the 38 working days from December 2026 to January 2027. A sample size based on resource constraints may not be large enough [@lakens2022sample], so Section 3.7 tests whether 2,500 posts are sufficient.

The annotated posts are divided once into a training set (72%), a validation set (14%), and a test set (14%), following the proportions of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. The split is stratified by humanitarian category, so each category has the same share in all three sets.

## Instruments to Be Used

The humanitarian category of each post is annotated according to the annotation guidelines (Appendix A), which define the categories of Section 3.2. The two annotators annotate each post independently, and the inter-annotator agreement is measured with Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960coefficient]. The entity spans are annotated automatically by GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner] in zero-shot mode and are not checked by the annotators (Section 1.8.2).

The performance of each model is measured with F1-scores, following HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. For a humanitarian category or an entity type $c$,
$$P_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FP_c}, \qquad R_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c}, \qquad F1_c = \frac{2 P_c R_c}{P_c + R_c}$$
where $P_c$ is precision, $R_c$ is recall, $TP_c$ counts correct predictions of $c$, $FP_c$ counts wrong predictions of $c$, and $FN_c$ counts instances of $c$ that the model missed. Humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, and NER is scored with span-level micro-F1, in which a predicted span is correct only when its boundaries and type both match a labeled span. F1-scores are reported on a scale of 0 to 1, and differences between them in percentage points.

Transfer is measured on each task $t$ as the change $\Delta_t$ in F1-score from the single-task model, and on both tasks as the average change $\Delta_{\text{avg}}$,
$$\Delta_t = F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t} - F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}, \qquad \Delta_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_1 + \Delta_2\right)$$
where task 1 is humanitarian classification and task 2 is NER. A negative value shows negative transfer. The single-task score is the mean over the five runs of the single-task model for that task, since studies of multi-task optimizers measure the change against one single-task result for each task [@navon2022bargaining; @liu2023famo].

Computational cost is measured with training time and peak memory. Training time is the wall-clock time in seconds of the training steps of a run, and peak memory is the highest graphics processing unit (GPU) memory in mebibytes allocated by PyTorch during a run. During each run, the temperature, clock speed, and shared memory use of the GPU are recorded every second with nvidia-smi, so that runs slowed by overheating or by running out of GPU memory can be found and repeated (Section 3.9). The training time and peak memory of a model are their means across its main runs (Section 3.5). For the single-task models, training time is the sum for the two models, since both must be trained, and peak memory is the larger of the two, since they are trained one after the other. The overhead of an optimizer on either cost is its extra cost as a percentage of that of equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary; @liu2023famo].

## Procedure of Data Gathering

Posts are collected through the full-archive search of the X API, which charges US\$0.005 for each post it returns [@x2026pricing]. Each collection window (Section 3.2) is searched with the same query, which excludes reposts and quotes. The query contains the Tagalog keywords listed in Appendix B, which are related to tropical cyclones and their effects, such as *bagyo* (tropical cyclone) and *baha* (flood). Posts are collected in rounds, each sampled as described in Section 3.3, until about 2,500 posts meet the criteria in that section. These 2,500 posts cost at least US\$12.50.

Near-duplicate posts are removed following HumAID [@alam2021humaid], which keeps one of any two posts whose unigram and bigram counts have a cosine similarity above 0.75 after links, usernames, and non-ASCII characters are removed.

Users of X keep ownership of their posts but grant X a license to make them available to others [@x2026terms], so consent is not sought from each user. In the collected posts, usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and links are replaced with placeholders. The posts are stored only on the laptop used for training, and only the research group and an adjudicator from outside it have access to them, in line with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 [-@philippines2012dataprivacy]. As the developer policy of X requires, posts deleted on X are also deleted from the dataset, and only the post IDs are shared [@x2026devpolicy].

The two annotators annotate the humanitarian category of every post in doccano from December 2026 to January 2027. They are members of the research group who are fluent in Tagalog and English. They first annotate practice batches of 50 posts, collected in the same way but not in the sample, and the guidelines are revised after each until Cohen's kappa reaches at least .61, the lower bound of substantial agreement [@landis1977measurement]. The guidelines are then fixed, and the sample is annotated in eight batches of about 310 posts. The annotators settle disagreements by discussion, and those that remain are decided by the adjudicator, who works or does research in disaster management or crisis informatics and signs off on each batch.

The models are trained on the training set with LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl] and the settings in Appendix C, and the settings not listed there follow the defaults of LibMTL. Every model is trained for 10 epochs without early stopping, as in the benchmark of Xin et al. [-@xin2022mtohelp], and the checkpoint of the epoch with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary]. The validation score is the mean of the two F1-scores, or the F1-score of a single-task model, following HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner].

The embedding layer of the encoder, which holds most of its parameters, is frozen in every model, and the batch size is 8, because in a pilot run some of the optimizers did not fit in the 8 GB of GPU memory of the laptop when all layers were trained.

To tune the learning rate, each model except tuned static weighting is trained once with random seed 0 at the constant learning rates of 1, 3, 5, and 8 × 10^−5^, and the rate with the highest validation score is kept [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. Tuned static weighting searches its task weights together with the learning rate [@gama2026uniform]. At each learning rate, the weight of humanitarian classification is set to 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9 and the weight of NER to one minus that value [@xin2022mtohelp], which gives 36 runs.

Each multi-task model is then trained three times, with random seeds 1, 2, and 3, the number of runs that the training time allows, and each single-task model five times, with seeds 1 to 5. After the selection (Section 3.6), the final model is also trained with seeds 4 and 5, so that it has five runs to pair with those of the single-task models. Of the five runs of the final model, the one with the highest validation score is used in the prototype.

All runs are done with the laptop plugged in, in its Performance mode, and with other programs closed, so that training time is measured under the same condition in every run. The tuning runs and the main runs before the selection are each done in random order, so that changes in the condition of the laptop over time do not favor any optimizer.

## Statistical Treatment

The statistical tests first select the optimizer of the final model on the validation set, which answers the third research question, and then test the hypotheses of Chapter 1 on the test set, which answers part of the fourth.

A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) first tests whether the mean $\Delta_{\text{avg}}$ on the validation set (Section 3.4) differs among the 13 candidate models, following Tabuzo et al. [-@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. Each candidate contributes its three runs, so the F statistic has 12 and 26 degrees of freedom. If the ANOVA is significant at the .05 level, each of the other 12 optimizers is compared with equal weighting using Dunnett's test [@dunnett1955multiple], and an optimizer differs significantly from equal weighting when its adjusted $p$-value is below .05. If the ANOVA is not significant, no optimizer is treated as different from equal weighting. In either case, the difference between each optimizer and equal weighting is reported with a simultaneous 95% confidence interval from Dunnett's test.

The final model uses equal weighting unless another optimizer qualifies. An optimizer qualifies if its $\Delta_{\text{avg}}$ is significantly higher than that of equal weighting and its mean F1-score on neither task is lower than that of equal weighting. Among the qualifying optimizers, the final model uses the one with the highest mean $\Delta_{\text{avg}}$.

The hypotheses are tested separately for each task with a two-sided paired t-test on the test set. For each task, the null hypothesis states that the mean F1-score of the final model equals that of the single-task model, and the alternative hypothesis states that the two means differ (Chapter 1). Each pair is a run of the final model and the run of the single-task model with the same random seed, since both see the training set in the same order, which gives five pairs and 4 degrees of freedom. The null hypothesis is rejected for a task when $p$ is below .05, and the mean difference in F1-score is reported with its 95% confidence interval. For Dunnett's test and the paired t-test, a difference that is not significant is not taken to mean that the two models perform the same.

The ANOVA and Dunnett's test assume normally distributed residuals with equal variances across the candidate models, and the paired t-test assumes normally distributed differences. Normality is checked with the Shapiro–Wilk test and equal variances with Levene's test, and any violation is reported as a limitation. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which does not assume normality, is not used, because with only five pairs it cannot give a $p$-value below .05.

The other results are described with the mean and sample standard deviation across runs. These are the F1-scores of the single-task models (first research question), the F1-scores, $\Delta_t$, and $\Delta_{\text{avg}}$ of each candidate model on the validation set and its training time and peak memory (third research question), and the training time and peak memory of the final model and the single-task models (fourth research question). The total time of the tuning runs of each optimizer is also reported. Cohen's kappa is described with the bands of Landis and Koch [-@landis1977measurement].

## Data Analysis

The size of about 2,500 posts is based on annotation capacity rather than on a formula (Section 3.3), and a size chosen this way may not be large enough [@lakens2022sample]. Whether it is sufficient is therefore checked after training with a learning curve, which shows how the F1-scores change as more training posts are used [@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. In addition to its runs on the full training set, each single-task model is also trained on 25%, 50%, and 75% of the training set. Each smaller part is a random subset of the next larger one, stratified by humanitarian category, so that every part keeps the same mix of categories. Each part is trained with seeds 1 to 3 and the learning rate tuned on the full set, and the mean F1-score on the validation set is compared across the four sizes. The single-task models are used because each learns one task alone, so the curve shows how many posts each task needs without the effect of an optimizer. Following Miranda [-@miranda2023tlunifiedner], the check looks at the last step, from 75% to 100%. If the F1-score still rises by more than the standard deviation of the single-task model across its five runs, the rise is larger than the usual variation between runs, so the F1-scores have not leveled off and more posts would likely improve the models, which is reported as a limitation. If it rises by less, 75% of the training set already gives similar F1-scores, so the F1-scores have leveled off and the 2,500 posts are sufficient.

Because no model labels every post correctly, the errors of the final model are analyzed to show which posts it misinterprets and why. The analysis uses the predictions of the run in the prototype on the test set. The test set is drawn at random from the sample, stratified by humanitarian category (Section 3.3), and posts that seem likely to cause errors are not added to it on purpose, so the errors reflect the kinds of posts that the model is meant to label rather than only difficult ones. For humanitarian classification, a confusion matrix counts how often each category is mistaken for each other category. For NER, each wrong span is sorted by entity type and by kind of error, which is a missed span, an extra span, or a span with the wrong boundaries or type. The posts with errors are then read together to find what they have in common, such as their length, their mix of Tagalog and English, or their category. In the prototype, the model only suggests the category and the entities of each post, and the staff can correct a wrong label (@tbl-usecases), so an error of the model does not become a final decision.

## Software System Description

The software system of this study has two parts, a benchmarking system that prepares the dataset and trains, selects, and evaluates the models, and a prototype web application that runs the final model.

### System Structure

![System architecture of the benchmarking system and the prototype web application](figures/fig-3-1-system-architecture.pdf){#fig-system-architecture}

@fig-system-architecture is read from top to bottom. Its first two phases, data preparation and model training and selection, make up the benchmarking system and follow Sections 3.3 to 3.7. The third phase is the prototype web application (Section 3.8.2). The cylinders are stored data, and the slanted boxes are the input and output of the whole system.

The multi-task model follows the design shown in @fig-artifact of Chapter 1. The encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, has 22 layers and represents each token with 768 numbers [@aisingapore2026sealion]. As in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], the task head for classification joins the output for the first token with the mean output over all tokens and maps them to the ten categories with one linear layer, which gives a score for each category. The task head for NER maps the output for each token to the 21 BIO labels with one linear layer, which gives a score for each label, and only the first token of each word carries an NER label. Each single-task model uses the same encoder with only the task head of its own task, and it is trained with the loss of that task alone.

Both task heads are trained, as in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], with the cross-entropy loss, which is low when the model gives a high probability to the true label. For a batch of $B$ posts,
$$\mathcal{L}_1 = -\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} \log \hat{y}_{i,c_i}, \qquad \mathcal{L}_2 = -\frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{(i,k) \in K} \log \hat{y}_{i,k,\ell_{ik}}$$
where $\hat{y}_{i,c_i}$ is the probability that the model gives to the true category $c_i$ of post $i$, $K$ is the set of labeled tokens in the batch, and $\hat{y}_{i,k,\ell_{ik}}$ is the probability given to the true BIO label $\ell_{ik}$ of token $k$. Equal weighting and tuned static weighting add the two losses with the task weights of Chapter 2, with $w_1 = w_2 = 1$ for equal weighting, as in the code of LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl], and $w_2 = 1 - w_1$ for tuned static weighting (Section 3.5). GradNorm, MGDA, GradDrop, and IMTL take the task gradients at the output of the encoder, and PCGrad, CAGrad, Nash-MTL, and PCGrad with uncertainty weighting take them over all trained encoder parameters, following Kurin et al. [-@kurin2022unitary] and LibMTL. Eleven optimizers come from LibMTL, which also provides the training loop, and tuned static weighting and PCGrad with uncertainty weighting are written for this study from their published descriptions. In its first epoch, GradNorm in LibMTL adds the two losses with equal weights to record their starting values, and because its task gradients are taken at the output of the encoder, only the task heads are trained in that epoch. The study changes this so that the encoder is also trained in the first epoch, as in the algorithm of @chen2018gradnorm, which updates the whole model from the first step.

### Use Cases

@fig-use-cases shows the actors of the prototype web application and their use cases. The staff of a Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (DRRMO) are the main actor, and X is a secondary actor that supplies posts when the staff collect them directly. The researcher loads the trained model into the prototype and collects the labels that the staff correct. @tbl-usecases groups the use cases into five categories and describes each one and its result.

![Use case diagram of the prototype web application](figures/fig-3-2-use-cases.pdf){#fig-use-cases}

| Use Case Category | Use Case | Description | Result |
|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------------|:--------------------|
| Data input | Import posts | Loads a file of collected posts, or collects new posts from X using keywords and a date range set by the staff | The posts are stored in the database, ready to be analyzed |
| Classification and extraction | Analyze posts | Assigns one humanitarian category to each post and marks its entities with the trained multi-task model | Each post has a stored category and stored entity spans |
| Classification and extraction | View analyzed posts | Shows each post with its category and its entities highlighted | The staff see each post with its category and its entities highlighted |
| Classification and extraction | Correct a label | Lets the staff fix a wrong category or entity span | The corrected category or entity span replaces the predicted one and is saved as a correction |
| Monitoring | Filter posts | Shows only the posts of selected categories (such as requests or urgent needs), entity types, or dates | Only the posts that match the selected filters are shown |
| Monitoring | Mark post status | Marks a post as reviewed, forwarded to a response team, or not actionable | The new status of the post is saved |
| Reporting | View summary | Shows the number of posts per category and per location over time | The counts of posts per category and per location are shown over time |
| Reporting | Export report | Saves the filtered posts and summary counts as a file for situation reports | A CSV file of the filtered posts and summary counts is saved |
| Model management | Load trained model | Loads the final model into the prototype | The prototype uses the loaded model for every new analysis |
| Model management | Export corrected labels | Saves the labels corrected by the staff as a file that can be used to train future models | A JSON Lines file of the corrected posts is saved in the same format as the dataset (@tbl-dataset) |

: Use case specifications {#tbl-usecases tbl-colwidths="[17,20,38,25]"}

The prototype has three parts, shown in the last phase of @fig-system-architecture, all of which run on the computer of the study, so the posts that the staff analyze are not sent to an outside service. The interface, built with React, runs in a web browser and shows the posts, filters, summaries, and forms that the staff use. The server, built with FastAPI in Python, receives the requests from the interface, runs the final model with PyTorch to analyze new posts, and prepares the summaries and reports. The requests that the server accepts, such as a request to analyze a post, are described in an API specification that FastAPI generates in the standard OpenAPI format, and the specification is kept in the GitHub repository with the code. The database, PostgreSQL, stores the posts, their predicted and corrected labels, and their status.

The laptop in @tbl-hardware is the only machine used for training and measurement (Chapter 1). An internet connection is needed only to collect the posts and to download the encoder and the libraries. Training and measurement run without a connection. The code, the settings, and a file that fixes the version of every library are kept in a GitHub repository and archived on Zenodo with a permanent identifier. The labeled dataset is shared only in a form that complies with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 and the terms of the platforms. Posts from X are shared as post IDs, and posts from Facebook are not shared.

## Testing and Evaluation

Testing checks that the software works as designed before any results are gathered. The benchmarking system is tested so that its scores and measurements can be trusted, and the prototype is tested to confirm that each use case works. The models themselves are evaluated with the measures and tests of Sections 3.6 and 3.7.

**Unit testing.** Each part of the benchmarking code is tested with pytest on small examples whose correct output is worked out by hand. The tests check that the label of each word is placed on its first token, and that the scoring code gives the expected results for an exact span match, a wrong span boundary, a wrong entity type, and a category with no posts in the part being scored. They also check that each multi-task optimizer behaves as its original paper describes, for example that PCGrad leaves two gradients that do not conflict unchanged and that Nash-MTL changes its task weights during training. Further tests check that no post appears in more than one of the three parts and that only the final model and the single-task models can be scored on the test posts, and that two runs with the same random seed see the training posts in the same order.

**Integration testing.** The whole benchmarking system, from training to the result files, is run with pytest for all 15 models on a small part of the data. The tuning runs and the main runs start only after all unit and integration tests pass.

**Run validity.** During every run, the nvidia-smi records (Section 3.4) are checked for heat slowdowns, which the two slowdown fields report. When the memory of the graphics processor is nearly full, its driver also moves part of the memory of a run to the main memory, and the run continues at a lower speed [@nvidia2023sysmem]. The shared memory that Windows reports for the graphics processor, which includes this moved memory, is therefore also recorded. In the pilot run, it grew by at most 12 MiB while a model trained if the model fit in memory, and by 66 MiB or more when part of the memory was moved. A run in which either slowdown field shows a slowdown, or in which the shared memory grows by more than 50 MiB while the model trains, is repeated, because the slowdown would lengthen its training time or processing time.

**Stress testing.** Because the prototype may receive one post at a time or a whole file of posts, the best run of the final model and of each single-task model also label the test posts in batches of 1, 16, and 32 posts, timed as in Section 3.7, and the mean time per post and the peak memory are recorded for each batch size. These results are only described. The prototype server also labels the test posts repeatedly for one hour, and its memory use on the graphics processor and in the main memory is recorded every minute to check that it does not keep growing.

**Functional testing of the prototype.** Each use case in @tbl-usecases is tested with test cases that state an input, the expected result, and the actual result. A use case passes when the actual result matches the expected result in every test case. The tests are carried out by the researchers. Because the prototype is not evaluated with DRRMO staff, its intended users, the quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010 are not rated.
